headline: What Three Days on the Big 5 Floor Have Changed My Mind About
deck: Three arguments I would have made on Sunday morning that I would not make now.
excerpt: After three days at Big 5 Construct Saudi, three assumptions look weaker than they did on the opening morning: that a trade show is a legacy format, that construction is where the Saudi opportunity sits, and that contractors are buying artificial intelligence.
content:
Three days into Big 5 Construct Saudi, it is worth writing down which of my own assumptions have not survived the halls. Three of them have not.

The first is that the physical trade show is a legacy format kept alive by habit and hospitality budgets. It is not, and the reason is specific rather than sentimental. Everything a buyer is now being asked to check — build quality, finish, weight, the feel of a mechanism, whether two competing products actually differ where the datasheet says they do — is close to uncheckable on a screen. What stood out this week is how much of the floor activity is comparison rather than discovery. People arrive knowing the shortlist and use the halls to break the tie. That is a function a catalogue cannot perform, and it explains why more than 1,000 exhibitors from over 50 countries can still justify four days in Riyadh.

The second assumption to go is that construction is where the Saudi opportunity sits. Construction is where the attention sits. The opportunity increasingly sits after handover. The Kingdom has commissioned an extraordinary quantity of asset in a decade, and that estate has to be operated, maintained, monitored and improved for the next thirty years by somebody. Across conversations this week the companies with the most confident answers about their next five years were not the ones selling into the build. They were the ones selling into the operating phase — facilities management, energy management, condition monitoring, spare parts, service contracts.

The award list bears that out. The show's sustainability trail gave its Operational Sustainability recognition to Al-Futtaim Engineering Company for integrated facilities management, which is a service business, not a product. It is a small signal, but it is pointing the right way.

Related to that, facilities management itself has moved further than I expected. The category used to mean manpower, cleaning and a reactive maintenance desk. What is being sold on this floor is asset management, preventive and predictive maintenance, building management systems, sensors, work-order platforms, energy management, fire and life safety, condition monitoring and the reporting layer over all of it. The co-located Saudi FM & Clean event sitting beside the concrete and heavy equipment halls makes more sense at the end of the week than it did at the start.

The third assumption I have dropped is that contractors are in the market for artificial intelligence. They are not, or at least not under that name. A recurring pattern in conversations on the floor was that the moment a pitch reached the word intelligence, the buyer redirected it to a number. Fewer breakdowns. Faster completion. Less rework. Lower manpower dependency. Better quality. Safer sites. Energy savings. Lower lifecycle cost. Vendors who could translate their product into one of those got a second meeting. Vendors who could not got a brochure taken politely.

That is not scepticism about technology, and it would be a mistake to read it that way. The visible movement on this floor is away from traditional plant and towards automation, sensors, connected equipment, digital monitoring and machines that do repetitive or dangerous work. Robotics in particular has stopped being a conference topic and started attaching to specific tasks — spraying, finishing, grinding, trenching, reinforcement processing, inspection. Even concrete, which is as traditional as the industry gets, is becoming something you can instrument and read.

The difference is the framing. Buyers here are not asking whether a machine is intelligent. They are asking what it removes from a programme, a headcount or a maintenance budget, and whether the company selling it will still be reachable from Riyadh in three years. Those are the right questions, and a show that forces them to be asked in person is doing more work than I gave it credit for on Sunday.
author: Mo Qureshi
seoTitle: Three Days at Big 5 Saudi Changed Three Assumptions
seoDescription: The trade show format, where the Saudi opportunity sits and the appetite for artificial intelligence all look different after three days at Big 5.
